Lambing Season: Riding Safely Through Farming Country

From March to May, millions of lambs are born across the UK's upland farms. These tiny, uncoordinated animals have zero road sense and can appear on the road with no warning. For motorcycle tourers, lambing season adds a specific hazard that requires awareness and adjustment.

When and Where

  • Timing: Main lambing period is mid-March to early May, varying by region and altitude. Hill farms lamb later (April-May) than lowland farms (March-April).
  • Hotspot areas: The Yorkshire Dales, Lake District, Welsh mountains, Scottish Borders, Scottish Highlands, Peak District, North Pennines, and Dartmoor all have significant sheep farming.
  • Road types: Unfenced roads across open moorland and mountain areas are highest risk. Lambs and ewes wander freely.

The Hazards

  • Lambs on roads: Young lambs are skittish, unpredictable, and often run into the road rather than away from it. They may freeze in front of you.
  • Ewes crossing: Mother sheep will cross the road to reach their lambs regardless of traffic.
  • Groups: Sheep move in flocks. If one crosses, more will follow. Always assume there are more behind the one you can see.
  • Farm vehicles: Tractors, quad bikes, and Land Rovers associated with lambing may be on narrow roads at unexpected times.

Safe Riding Through Lambing Country

  • Reduce speed on unfenced roads through sheep farming areas
  • Be especially cautious around blind corners on rural roads — sheep may be standing in the road just out of sight
  • If you see one sheep, scan for others. They rarely travel alone.
  • Sound your horn gently at a distance to encourage sheep to move — don't blast past them at speed
  • If sheep are blocking the road, stop and wait. They'll move eventually. Getting off the bike and walking towards them gently encourages them along.
Hitting a sheep at speed is serious — for both you and the animal. A ewe weighs 60-80kg and an impact at touring speed can cause a crash. Slow down, stay alert, and give the farmland the respect it deserves. You're riding through someone's workplace and livelihood.

Legal Responsibility

If you hit a sheep, you are legally required to report it to the police (Section 170 of the Road Traffic Act 1988 covers injury to certain animals, including sheep). Stop, check for injury, and contact the nearest farm or police. Don't ride away.

Building Your Tradition

If you don't have a New Year riding tradition, start one. Choose a route, a destination, or a ritual that you'll repeat each year. Some riders always visit the same café. Others ride the same loop from home. Some photograph their bike at the same location each January 1st to create a year-on-year comparison.

Whatever your tradition, the act of riding on January 1st anchors your identity as a motorcyclist. It's a statement of intent: this year, like every year, will be a riding year. And from that first ride, the momentum builds through the dark weeks of winter towards the spring and the long touring season ahead.

Making It Special

Elevate your first ride from a quick loop to a memorable experience. Choose a destination that's meaningful — the café where you planned your first tour, the viewpoint where you proposed, or the road where you learned to ride. Ritual and repetition give the New Year ride significance beyond simple mileage.

Document your first ride with photos. A picture of your bike on January 1st each year creates a visual diary of your riding life — changing bikes, changing gear, the same familiar roads in different winter conditions. After a few years, these photos become a treasured record of your riding journey.

If you ride with friends, make the New Year ride a group tradition. A regular crew, a regular route, and a regular finish at the same pub creates shared history and strengthens friendships built on a common passion. The stories accumulated over years of New Year rides become part of your group's folklore.

faq.q: When is lambing season in the UK?
faq.a: The main lambing period runs from mid-March to early May, though it varies by region and altitude. Lowland farms tend to lamb in March and April, while hill farms lamb later, into April and May, because of colder upland conditions. The hazard is present across most of the touring season's opening months.

faq.q: Where are the worst areas for sheep on the road?
faq.a: The Yorkshire Dales, Lake District, Welsh mountains, Scottish Borders, Highlands, Peak District, North Pennines, and Dartmoor all have significant sheep farming. Unfenced roads across open moorland are the highest risk, as lambs and ewes wander freely and can appear on the tarmac with no warning.

faq.q: What should I do if sheep block the road?
faq.a: Stop and wait; they will move eventually. Sounding your horn gently from a distance encourages them along, but never blast past at speed. If they refuse to shift, getting off the bike and walking slowly towards them usually moves them on. Always assume more sheep are behind the one you can see.

faq.q: What are my legal duties if I hit a sheep?
faq.a: You are legally required to report it to the police. Section 170 of the Road Traffic Act 1988 covers injury to certain animals, including sheep. Stop, check for injury, and contact the nearest farm or the police. Do not simply ride away.
